metaTitle: Should You Put a Photo on Your Resume or CV? By Country

content:
It depends on where you are applying and in which industry. In the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada a photo on a CV is unusual and often discouraged, while in much of continental Europe, the Middle East and parts of Asia it is common or expected. When in doubt, leave it off the resume and make sure your LinkedIn photo is excellent, because that is where the recruiter will look anyway.

This guide sets out the country conventions, why some markets actively discourage a photo, the industries where one is expected regardless, and what the photo must do wherever it ends up living.

Should you put a photo on your resume or CV?

Follow the norm of the country and the industry you are applying in, not the country you live in. If the market discourages photos, leave it off: a photo there adds bias risk and no upside. If the market expects one, include a recent, evenly lit head and shoulders photo that looks like you today.

Either way, assume the hiring manager will open your LinkedIn profile within minutes of reading the CV, so the photo they see there has to be right.

At a glance

RegionPhoto on the CVWhat to do
United States, United Kingdom, CanadaUnusual and often discouragedLeave it off; put the effort into LinkedIn
Much of continental EuropeCommon or expectedInclude a professional head and shoulders photo
Middle EastCommon or expectedInclude one; conservative dress and background
Parts of AsiaCommon or expected, sometimes formalInclude one; check the employer's application format
Acting, modelling, some client-facing rolesExpected everywhereInclude one; it is part of the application
Where recruiters look regardlessLinkedInA profile with a photo gets up to 21 times more views

Which countries expect a photo on a CV?

There is no global rule, only local habits. In the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, a photo on a resume is unusual and many employers and recruiters prefer not to receive one. In much of continental Europe, the Middle East and parts of Asia, a photo is a normal part of the document and its absence can look like an oversight.

The safest source of truth is the employer's own application format. A structured application form with a photo field tells you a photo is expected. A job advert that says "no photos" or an applicant tracking system that strips images tells you the opposite.

If you are applying across borders, keep two versions of your CV: one with a photo for the markets that expect it and one without for the markets that do not. It takes five minutes and avoids sending the wrong signal in either direction.

Why do some markets discourage photos on resumes?

The concern is bias. A photo tells a reader your approximate age, ethnicity, sex and sometimes your religion or a disability before they have read a single line about your work. Employers in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada often ask for no photo so that those factors cannot influence a shortlist, and so that they cannot be accused of letting them.

The research on faces explains why this is a real worry rather than a formality. Princeton psychologists Willis and Todorov found that people form judgements of trustworthiness, competence, likeability and attractiveness from a face after roughly 100 milliseconds of exposure, and that looking longer mostly makes people more confident rather than more accurate. A photo on a CV triggers that judgement before your experience gets a hearing.

So in those markets, leaving the photo off is not a missed opportunity. It is the convention, and including one can read as not knowing the convention.

Which industries expect a photo regardless of country?

Some roles are about how you present in person, and there the photo is part of the application everywhere. The clearest cases are:

  • Acting and performance: the headshot is a standard attachment and casting decisions start from it.
  • Modelling and on-camera presenting: the photo is the product, and a full set is usually expected.
  • Some client-facing roles: front-of-house hospitality, cabin crew, brand ambassadors and certain sales positions, where employers often ask for a photo in the application form.

Outside those, treat the country convention as the default. If a recruiter or job advert asks for a photo, send one. If they do not, and you are in a market that discourages it, do not volunteer one.

What should a resume photo look like where one is expected?

The same rules as a LinkedIn photo, because it is doing the same job. LinkedIn's own profile photo guidelines require that the photo reflects your likeness, and that is the right standard for a CV too: recent, recognisably you, and not a flattering stranger.

In practice that means a head and shoulders crop, your face filling most of the frame, even light with no hard shadows across the face, a plain or softly blurred background, and the clothes you would wear to the interview. Save it as a small, sharp image so the file does not balloon and place it top right or top left where the format expects it.

What it must not be: a holiday photo cropped from a group, a selfie in a car, a heavily filtered image, or a picture from ten years ago. Research on face perception shows that different photos of the same person produce substantially different first impressions, with lighting, pose and expression moving the judgement, so the specific photo you choose matters more than most people assume.

Will recruiters look you up on LinkedIn anyway?

Yes, and this is the reason the CV question matters less than it seems. Whether or not your resume carries a photo, the person reading it will very likely search your name, and LinkedIn is the first result they open. Your profile photo becomes your resume photo whether you put one on the document or not.

LinkedIn Sales Solutions reports that members with a profile photo get up to 21 times more profile views and 9 times more connection requests than members without one. A recruiter who lands on a profile with no photo, or a poor one, has less reason to stay and read.

That shifts the effort. Spend less time deciding whether to paste a photo into a Word document and more time making sure the photo on your LinkedIn profile is recent, well lit and looks like you. If you need one this week, a set of LinkedIn headshots from Picturesk is generated from your own selfies and delivered by email in about an hour.

Why does the photo have to be right wherever it lives?

Because the reader decides fast and does not revisit. The Princeton work found the judgement forms in around a tenth of a second, and the Association for Psychological Science's overview of the field notes that these snap impressions are fast, hard to shift and influential on what happens next. A CV cannot argue with an impression that was made before the first bullet point.

The good news is that the levers are simple. Even light, a relaxed and genuine expression, a clean background and a recent photo all push the impression in your favour. A photo that fails on any of those pushes it the other way, however strong the experience underneath it is.

How do you decide? A short checklist

  1. Check the country. United States, United Kingdom or Canada: leave it off. Continental Europe, Middle East, parts of Asia: include one.
  2. Check the industry. Acting, modelling or a client-facing role that asks for a photo: include one regardless of country.
  3. Check the employer's format. A photo field means yes; a "no photos" note or an image-stripping application system means no.
  4. When still in doubt, leave it off the CV.
  5. Whatever you decide, update your LinkedIn photo so it is recent, evenly lit, head and shoulders, and looks like you in person.

Keep the photo and the CV consistent. If the recruiter sees one face on the document and a visibly different one on LinkedIn, they will trust neither, and the whole point of the photo was to build trust.

faqs.question: Should I put a photo on my resume in the US?
faqs.answer: No, in most cases. A photo on a US resume is unusual and many employers prefer not to receive one because of bias concerns. Leave it off unless the role is in acting, modelling or a client-facing job that specifically asks for a photo, and make sure your LinkedIn photo is strong instead.

faqs.question: Is a photo expected on a CV in Europe?
faqs.answer: In much of continental Europe, yes. A head and shoulders photo is a normal part of the CV and leaving it out can look like an oversight. Check the employer's application format first, and where a photo is expected use a recent, evenly lit image that looks like you today.

faqs.question: What should a CV photo look like?
faqs.answer: The same as a good LinkedIn photo: recent, head and shoulders, evenly lit, plain background, interview clothing, and recognisably you. LinkedIn's own guideline says the photo must reflect your likeness, and that is the right test for a CV too. No group crops, car selfies or heavy filters.

faqs.question: Do recruiters check LinkedIn if my resume has no photo?
faqs.answer: Almost always. Recruiters search your name and LinkedIn is usually the first result, so your profile photo becomes your resume photo either way. LinkedIn Sales Solutions reports profiles with a photo get up to 21 times more views, which is why that photo deserves more effort than the CV question.
